lesson.title: Three Resistors, No Center: The Delta Configuration
lesson.summary: A delta configuration connects three resistors in a closed triangle between three terminals with no shared center node, a pattern common in three phase power windings and resistor attenuator networks.
lesson.body:
A delta configuration, named for its triangular shape and written with the Greek letter capital delta, connects three resistors directly between three terminals, with no common center node anywhere. Label the terminals A, B, and C. The delta consists of resistor R_AB directly between A and B, resistor R_BC directly between B and C, and resistor R_CA directly between C and A. In three phase power systems this same wiring pattern is called a mesh connection, and in filter and attenuator design it is sometimes called a pi configuration. Structurally, a delta is literally a small loop of three branches and three nodes, so it is worth noticing this is exactly the kind of mesh described earlier in this chapter sequence, just drawn as a standalone building block instead of as part of a larger network.

Because there is no center node, finding the resistance between any two delta terminals takes a small bit of circuit reasoning rather than a single obvious formula. Between terminals A and B, current has two possible routes: straight across through R_AB, or the long way around, from A through R_CA to C, then from C through R_BC to B. Since terminal C is not connected to anything else, that second route forces current through R_CA and R_BC in series. The direct resistor and the long way around route are therefore in parallel with each other.

Take a balanced delta where all three resistors are equal: R_AB = R_BC = R_CA = 30 ohm. The resistance between terminals A and B is R_AB in parallel with (R_BC plus R_CA), which is 30 ohm in parallel with 60 ohm. That works out to (30 times 60) divided by (30 plus 60), or 1800 divided by 90, which is 20 ohm. That 20 ohm figure is the resistance an ohmmeter would actually read across any two terminals of this delta, with the third terminal left disconnected.

Delta connections show up constantly in three phase power, where motor and generator windings are often wired line to line in a delta, which has the practical advantage of needing no neutral wire at all. The same triangular pattern appears in resistive attenuator pads used in audio and RF equipment, where the three resistors are chosen to set both an impedance and an attenuation level simultaneously. What a delta configuration does not offer, though, is a convenient center reference point, which makes writing simple expressions for internal currents harder than it needs to be.

That missing center point is exactly what the wye configuration, covered next, provides. It turns out a wye network can be built that behaves identically at all three terminals to a given delta, including reproducing that same 20 ohm terminal to terminal resistance found here, even though internally the two networks look nothing alike. That equivalence, and the exact numbers connecting them, is the subject of the delta wye transformation shortly after.
